etymology: From body (a complete and ordered whole) and divinity (the science of God, theology); a settled term for a systematic exposition of the whole of Christian doctrine.
biblical_def: A “body of divinity” is a full and orderly treatment of the whole counsel of God, setting forth in connected form the doctrines of Scripture concerning God, man, sin, Christ, salvation, the church, and the last things. The phrase belongs especially to the Reformed and Puritan tradition, which produced many such works, the most beloved being Thomas Watson’s A Body of Divinity, lectures upon the Westminster Shorter Catechism, prized for their warmth and quaint, pungent illustration. The aim of a body of divinity is not bare information but the knowledge of God unto godliness; it follows the conviction that doctrine and life are not divided, that sound theology is the handmaid of holiness, and that the catechized believer is the established believer. Such works typically follow the order of a confession or catechism, expounding each head of doctrine, answering objections, and pressing application upon the conscience. The dictionary commends the body of divinity as the proper fruit of a church that takes the whole counsel of God seriously: not a few favorite themes endlessly repeated, but the entire system of truth taught, learned, confessed, and obeyed. To know a little of everything God has revealed, and that little well ordered, is the laborer’s armory and the believer’s stability.
webster_summary: A complete and ordered exposition of the whole of Christian doctrine; especially Thomas Watson’s beloved Puritan exposition of the Westminster Shorter Catechism.
webster_full: BODY OF DIVINITY, a systematic treatment of the entire compass of Christian doctrine.
From divinity, the older English term for theology, the science of God and divine things.
Typically follows the order of a confession or catechism through each head of doctrine.
The most cherished example is Thomas Watson’s, lectures on the Westminster Shorter Catechism.
Designed not for mere knowledge but for the knowledge of God unto godliness and stability.
scriptures: For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
corruption_summary: Systematic theology is dismissed as cold or divisive by an age that prizes vague spirituality over ordered truth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the whole counsel of God is to be declared, learned, and held in an ordered form. A body of divinity stands against the modern preference for a handful of comforting themes endlessly repeated, and against the notion that doctrine divides while experience unites. Watson and his fellows knew that the most affectionate, practical, and stable Christians are the best instructed ones.

Where a corruption presses, it is the false opposition of head and heart—the suspicion that systematic doctrine quenches devotion. The Puritan body of divinity is the standing refutation: its pages are at once rigorous and warm, doctrinal and devotional, pressing every truth home upon the conscience. To know God systematically is not to know Him coldly; it is to love Him with the mind as well as the heart, as the great commandment requires.
roots_summary: The term joins the idea of a complete body with the old word for theology, naming an ordered whole of Christian truth.
roots_lines: English body — a complete, organized whole, used of a connected system.
English divinity — the science of God, theology, from Latin divinitas.
The phrase parallels Latin corpus theologiae, a body or corpus of theology.
Akin in aim to the catechism and the confession, but fuller in exposition.
Watson, Ussher, and others gave the title to their systematic works.
usage: A new believer is often pointed to a body of divinity to gain the whole frame of Christian doctrine.
Pastors recommend Watson’s as a warm, quotable companion to the Shorter Catechism.
The phrase is used to distinguish a complete systematic work from a treatise on one doctrine.

etymology: From marrow (the inmost, richest substance) and theology; a rendering of the Latin Medulla Theologiae of William Ames.
biblical_def: The Marrow of Theology (Latin Medulla Theologiae) is the celebrated systematic theology of the English Puritan William Ames, first published early in the seventeenth century and long used as a textbook in the Reformed academies of the Netherlands and in early New England. Ames famously defined theology as “the doctrine of living to God,” binding doctrine and practice together at the root: the knowledge of God is never a bare science but is ordered to godliness and obedience. The work divides into faith (what we are to believe of God) and observance (how we are to live unto Him), reflecting that practical, experimental cast which marks the whole Puritan tradition. Ames stood in the line of Perkins and shaped the piety of generations, including the founders of the New England churches who carried his book across the Atlantic. The title “marrow” signals the method: not endless dispute but the inmost substance of divinity, compressed, ordered, and pressed toward life. The dictionary commends Ames’s definition as a corrective to every theology that grows abstract, learned, and lifeless. Theology that does not issue in living to God has lost its marrow; it has become a skeleton of notions. The end of all true divinity is the worship and obedience of the living God.
webster_summary: William Ames’s influential Puritan systematic theology, which defined divinity as “the doctrine of living to God” and bound doctrine inseparably to godliness.
webster_full: MARROW OF THEOLOGY, the English title of William Ames’s Latin Medulla Theologiae.
A systematic divinity widely used in Reformed academies and in early New England.
Famous for defining theology as “the doctrine of living to God.”
Divided into faith, what to believe, and observance, how to live unto God.
Shaped the experimental, practical piety of the Puritan and early American churches.
scriptures: Tit 1:1
Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness;
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
Joh 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
Psa 16:8
I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
corruption_summary: Theology is divorced from life and reduced to academic technique, the very fault Ames’s definition was framed to prevent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Ames’s root definition: theology is the doctrine of living to God. Against the modern academic study of religion as a detached science, and against the popular reduction of faith to feeling, Ames holds the two together—sound doctrine ordered wholly toward obedience and worship. The acknowledging of the truth is, in Paul’s phrase, “after godliness.”

Where corruption presses, it is the split between the seminary and the closet, the lecture and the life. Ames’s “marrow” refuses the split: divinity that does not teach a man to live to God has missed its end. The corrective is not less theology but theology rightly aimed—every doctrine learned that it may be lived, every truth confessed that God may be served, the whole of divinity bending toward the great purpose for which man was made: to glorify God and to enjoy Him.
roots_summary: The image of marrow names the inmost substance of theology, compressed and aimed at living to God.
roots_lines: English marrow — the inmost, richest substance, used figuratively for the essence of a thing.
Latin medulla — marrow, pith; the original title word in Ames’s Medulla Theologiae.
Greek theologia — the word or doctrine concerning God.
Ames’s definition: theology as doctrina Deo vivendi, the doctrine of living to God.
The title signals essence over dispute—the marrow, not the bones, of divinity.
usage: Ames’s definition of theology is quoted to insist that doctrine and godliness are one.
The Marrow is cited as a foundational text of New England Puritan divinity.
Teachers use it to warn against theology that grows abstract and ceases to serve obedience.

etymology: From religious (pertaining to true worship and godliness) and affections (the inclinations and movements of the will); the title of Jonathan Edwards’s great treatise.
biblical_def: A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections is Jonathan Edwards’s searching examination of the nature of true religion, written in the wake of the Great Awakening to distinguish the genuine work of the Spirit from its counterfeits. Edwards’s thesis is that “true religion, in great part, consists in holy affections”—that real godliness is not cold notional assent, nor mere outward duty, but the lively engagement of the heart, the will moved toward God in love, joy, hope, fear, and grief over sin. Yet Edwards is equally concerned to expose false affections: high feelings, fluent talk, abundant tears, and sudden raptures prove nothing in themselves, for hypocrites may have them all. He lays down distinguishing marks of gracious affections, chief among them their arising from the loveliness of divine things themselves, their tendency to humble the soul, and supremely their fruit in Christian practice—a holy life is the great evidence of a renewed heart. The dictionary commends the Affections as the finest anatomy of experimental religion in the English tongue, holding the narrow path between dead orthodoxy on the one hand and unbridled enthusiasm on the other. The heart must be engaged, but the test of the heart’s engagement is a transformed life.
webster_summary: Jonathan Edwards’s classic treatise on the nature of true religion, holding that genuine godliness consists in holy affections proved by their fruit in a holy life.
webster_full: RELIGIOUS AFFECTIONS, the title of Jonathan Edwards’s treatise on the nature of true religion.
Written after the Great Awakening to distinguish the Spirit’s work from its counterfeits.
Holds that true religion in great part consists in holy affections of the heart.
Exposes false affections—feelings, fluency, and raptures that prove nothing in themselves.
Names Christian practice, a holy life, as the chief sign of gracious affections.
scriptures: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory:
Mat 7:20
Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
Psa 42:1
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
Deu 6:5
And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
corruption_summary: Edwards’s careful balance is broken on both sides—by dead orthodoxy that despises feeling, and by emotionalism that mistakes excitement for grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Edwards’s balance: true religion engages the affections, yet the test of those affections is not their intensity but their fruit in a holy life. Against the modern revival culture that measures God’s work by the height of feeling and the size of the response, Edwards insists that “the degree of religion is to be judged by the fixedness and strength of the habit that is exercised in affection, whereby holy affections are habitual.”

The corruption runs in two directions. On one side stands a dead orthodoxy that prides itself on doctrine while the heart lies cold, despising affection as mere emotionalism. On the other stands an unbridled enthusiasm that mistakes goosebumps and tears for regeneration and trusts a moment of high feeling as conversion. Edwards refutes both: the heart must truly be moved, but moved by the loveliness of God Himself, humbled rather than puffed up, and proved by a changed life. By their fruits ye shall know them.
roots_summary: The title joins true religion with the affections, the movements of the will, which Edwards held to be the seat of real godliness.
roots_lines: English affection — an inclination or vigorous movement of the will toward or against an object.
For Edwards the affections are “the more vigorous and sensible exercises of the inclination and will of the soul.”
Distinguished from mere passions or bodily emotions, though often attended by them.
Religious — pertaining to the true worship and service of God.
The title names the seat of true religion: not bare intellect, but the heart engaged toward God.
usage: Edwards’s Affections is the standard work cited in discerning true from false conversion.
Its insistence on Christian practice as the chief sign is preached against easy-believism.
The treatise is used to correct both cold orthodoxy and revivalist emotionalism.

etymology: From know (Old English cnāwan, to perceive, recognize, be acquainted with) and God; the title of J. I. Packer’s celebrated study of the knowledge of God.
biblical_def: Knowing God is the widely read twentieth-century study by the Reformed Anglican theologian J. I. Packer, which set before a modern readership the great Puritan conviction that the chief business of man is to know God. Packer drew the crucial distinction between knowing about God and knowing God Himself—the first a matter of information, the second a matter of acquaintance, communion, and love. He expounded the attributes of God in a manner at once doctrinal and devotional, treating God’s majesty, wisdom, grace, severity, jealousy, and supremely His adopting fatherly love, and pressing always toward the practical end that those who know God are bold, contented, and zealous. The book recovered for many the Puritan vision that theology is for doxology and obedience, that the deepest knowledge of God humbles and warms the soul, and that to know God is the highest of all sciences and the sweetest of all consolations. The dictionary commends the central thesis as thoroughly biblical: eternal life itself is defined by Christ as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent. To know God is the end for which man was made; all lesser knowledge is dust beside it; and such knowledge is given only through Christ the Mediator, by the Spirit, in the Scriptures.
webster_summary: J. I. Packer’s modern classic recovering the Puritan vision that man’s chief business is to know God Himself—not merely about Him—in communion and love.
webster_full: KNOWING GOD, the title of J. I. Packer’s widely read study of the knowledge of God.
Distinguishes knowing about God, mere information, from knowing God, communion and love.
Expounds the divine attributes in a manner both doctrinal and devotional.
Recovers the Puritan conviction that theology serves doxology and obedience.
Presses the end that those who know God are bold, contented, and zealous for Him.
scriptures: Joh 17:3

Jer 9:23
Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
Php 3:8
Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord:
corruption_summary: The knowledge of God is reduced to academic information or to mystical feeling, missing the personal communion Scripture means.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Packer’s distinction: a man may know much about God and yet not know God, as a man may know much about a king he has never met. Eternal life is not the accumulation of theological data but the personal knowledge of the true God in Christ. Against an academic religion of information and a vague spirituality of feeling alike, Scripture sets communion: to understand and know the LORD.

Where a corruption presses, it is the modern severing of the knowledge of God from doctrine—as if one could know God personally while remaining indifferent to who He has revealed Himself to be. Packer answers that we know God only as He has made Himself known, through His attributes, His acts, and His Son; there is no knowing God apart from the truth about God. The warmest communion rests on the soundest doctrine; the two are not rivals but one.
roots_summary: The title turns on the biblical sense of knowing—not mere information but covenant acquaintance and love.
roots_lines: Hebrew yāda’ — to know, often of intimate, covenant, personal acquaintance, not bare information.
Greek ginōskō — to know by experience and relationship, used in John 17:3 of eternal life.
English know — from Old English cnāwan, to perceive, recognize, be acquainted with.
The biblical idiom distinguishes knowing about God from knowing God Himself.
Such knowledge is mediated by Christ, given by the Spirit, drawn from the Scriptures.
usage: Packer’s distinction between knowing about God and knowing God is widely quoted in discipleship.
The book is recommended as a devotional study of the divine attributes.
Its thesis is cited to unite sound doctrine with warm communion.

etymology: From redemption (a buying back, deliverance by payment of a price) with the twin terms accomplished (finished, achieved) and applied (brought home, made effectual); the title of John Murray’s study.
biblical_def: Redemption Accomplished and Applied is the compact and influential study of the work of Christ by the Scottish-American Reformed theologian John Murray. Its two-part structure names a vital biblical distinction: redemption was first accomplished by Christ in His obedience, death, and resurrection, and is then applied by the Holy Spirit to the elect in the order of salvation. The first part treats the atonement—its necessity, nature, perfection, and especially its definite, particular design, that Christ did not die to make all men savable but to save His own people effectually. The second part traces the application: calling, regeneration, faith and repentance, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, and glorification, in their biblical order and mutual connection. Murray’s great service is to hold accomplishment and application together—the cross actually secured the salvation of those for whom it was offered, and the Spirit infallibly applies what the Son infallibly purchased. The dictionary commends the work as a clear modern statement of definite atonement and the Reformed order of salvation, against every scheme that makes the cross a mere possibility awaiting the sinner’s decision to render it effectual. What Christ accomplished, the Spirit applies; none for whom He died will fail to be saved.
webster_summary: John Murray’s study of the work of Christ in two movements—redemption accomplished at the cross (definite atonement) and applied by the Spirit in the order of salvation.
webster_full: REDEMPTION ACCOMPLISHED AND APPLIED, the title of John Murray’s study of Christ’s saving work.
Part one treats the atonement—its necessity, nature, perfection, and definite, particular design.
Part two traces the application: calling, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption, and the rest.
Holds that the Spirit infallibly applies what the Son infallibly purchased.
A clear modern statement of definite atonement and the Reformed order of salvation.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
Eph 1:7
In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace;
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
corruption_summary: The universal-atonement scheme makes the cross a mere possibility, severing what Christ accomplished from what is actually applied.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Murray recovers is the unbreakable bond between accomplishment and application. Christ did not die to make men merely savable; He died to save His sheep, and what He purchased the Spirit applies. The golden chain of Romans 8—predestinated, called, justified, glorified—has no broken links: not one for whom Christ died is finally lost.

The corruption Murray answers is the universal or general atonement of Arminian and Amyraldian schemes, in which Christ died equally for all, the cross secures the salvation of none in particular, and its effect waits upon the sinner’s free decision. This severs accomplishment from application and makes the most precious blood ever shed a mere possibility that men may render vain. The dictionary holds with Murray and with Owen’s Death of Death: the atonement is definite, particular, and effectual, securing infallibly the salvation of the elect.
roots_summary: The two title words mark the two movements of salvation—the price paid by Christ and the purchase brought home by the Spirit.
roots_lines: English redemption — a buying back, deliverance by the payment of a ransom price.
Greek apolutrōsis — redemption, release secured by a ransom, as in Ephesians 1:7.
Accomplished — finished, achieved; echoing Christ’s “It is finished.”
Applied — brought home and made effectual by the Holy Spirit to the elect.
The pairing names the work of the Son and the work of the Spirit as one undivided salvation.
usage: Murray’s book is a standard modern text for the doctrine of definite atonement.
Its two-part scheme is used to teach the order of salvation in seminaries.
The title phrase is quoted to insist that the cross actually secured, not merely offered, salvation.

etymology: From Reformed (of the churches of the Reformation in the Calvinist line) and dogmatics (the ordered science of the church’s settled doctrines, from Greek dogma, a decree); the title of Herman Bavinck’s great system.
biblical_def: Reformed Dogmatics is the magisterial four-volume systematic theology of the Dutch theologian Herman Bavinck, completed in the early twentieth century and reckoned among the finest systematic works the Reformed tradition has produced. Bavinck treats the whole compass of Christian doctrine—the foundations and sources of theology, the doctrine of God, creation and providence, sin and salvation in Christ, and the last things—with vast learning, catholic breadth, and a deep rootedness in Scripture and the Reformed confessions. His genius lay in synthesis: he engaged the whole history of Christian thought, ancient and medieval and Protestant, and the philosophy and science of his own day, yet bent all to the service of confessional Reformed truth. A favorite Bavinck theme is that “grace restores nature”—that redemption does not destroy the created order but heals and perfects it. The dictionary commends Bavinck as a model of theology that is at once rigorously confessional and broadly learned, never sectarian and never compromising. “Dogmatics” is not a cold or arbitrary word, as the modern ear hears it, but the ordered confession of what God has revealed, the church’s settled understanding of the faith once delivered to the saints, set forth with reverence for the God whose truth it handles.
webster_summary: Herman Bavinck’s monumental four-volume Reformed systematic theology, marked by vast learning, confessional fidelity, and the theme that grace restores nature.
webster_full: REFORMED DOGMATICS, the four-volume systematic theology of Herman Bavinck.
From dogmatics, the ordered science of the church’s settled doctrines.
Treats the whole of Christian doctrine with vast learning and confessional fidelity.
Engages the full history of Christian thought, bending all to Reformed truth.
Famous for the theme that grace does not destroy but restores and perfects nature.

corruption_summary: The word “dogmatics” is heard as arbitrary or oppressive, and systematic theology is dismissed as a relic in an anti-doctrinal age.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that “dogma” means the church’s settled confession of revealed truth, not human opinion imposed by force. Bavinck’s dogmatics is the ordered exposition of the faith once delivered to the saints. Against an age that uses “dogmatic” as an insult and prizes open-ended uncertainty, the church confesses that God has spoken and that His truth may be known, ordered, and held with conviction.

Where corruption presses, it is the modern preference for theology as endless conversation rather than settled confession—the notion that to affirm doctrine with certainty is arrogant or closed-minded. Bavinck answers with the breadth of true catholicity married to the firmness of true confession: he listens to all, learns from much, and concludes with the Reformed faith, because the question is not who is most open but what God has revealed. Grace restores nature; truth settles the mind; and the glory is God’s alone.
roots_summary: The title joins the Reformed confession with the word for ordered doctrine, naming theology as the church’s settled science of revealed truth.
roots_lines: Greek dogma — a decree, an established opinion or settled teaching.
Dogmatics — the ordered science of the church’s confessed doctrines.
Reformed — of the churches recovered to biblical truth in the sixteenth century, in the Calvinist line.
Bavinck’s watchword: gratia naturam non tollit sed perficit, grace does not abolish but perfects nature.
Distinguished from biblical theology by its systematic, topical arrangement of doctrine.
usage: Bavinck’s Reformed Dogmatics is a standard advanced text in Reformed seminaries.
His “grace restores nature” is widely cited in discussions of creation and redemption.
The work is held up as a model of learned yet confessional systematic theology.

etymology: From art (a skilled method or discipline) and prophesying, here in the older English sense of expounding and applying Scripture in preaching; the title of William Perkins’s manual.
biblical_def: The Art of Prophesying is the brief and seminal manual of preaching by William Perkins, the Cambridge Puritan often called the father of the Puritan movement. By “prophesying” Perkins meant not the foretelling of the future but the public preaching of the Word—the opening and applying of Scripture, as the term is used in First Corinthians fourteen. Perkins set forth a plain, ordered method that shaped generations of Puritan preachers: read the text rightly from the Scriptures, give the plain sense and meaning by Scripture itself, collect a few profitable points of doctrine from the natural sense, and then apply the doctrine to the life and manners of the hearers. His celebrated taxonomy of hearers—the ignorant and unteachable, the teachable ignorant, those who have knowledge but are not humbled, the humbled, the believers, and the fallen—trained ministers to apply the Word to every spiritual condition. He insisted that the preacher hide human eloquence so that the power of the Spirit and the Word might appear, that “the preaching of the Word is the testimony of God, and the profession of the knowledge of Christ, and not of human wisdom.” The dictionary commends Perkins’s plain style as the recovery of preaching as the chief means of grace: the Word opened, doctrine drawn, and conscience pressed, in dependence on the Spirit.
webster_summary: William Perkins’s foundational Puritan manual of preaching, teaching the plain method of opening Scripture, drawing doctrine, and applying it to every condition of hearer.
webster_full: THE ART OF PROPHESYING, William Perkins’s seminal manual of preaching.
Uses prophesying in its older sense: the public preaching and applying of the Word.
Teaches the plain method—read, give the sense, collect doctrine, apply to the hearers.
Famous for its taxonomy of seven kinds of hearers and how to address each.
Insists the preacher hide his own eloquence that the Spirit and the Word may appear.
scriptures: But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Plain expository preaching is displaced by entertainment, oratory, and felt-need talks that no longer open and apply the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Perkins’s plain method: the preacher’s task is to open the text, draw out its doctrine, and apply it to the consciences of his hearers, hiding his own cleverness that the Spirit and the Word may have free course. Against pulpit performance, motivational speaking, and the felt-need talk that uses a verse as a springboard and never returns to it, the art of prophesying is simply to preach the Word.

Where a corruption presses, it is the modern flight from the plain style into either dry lecture or theatrical entertainment—the first forgetting application, the second forgetting the text. Perkins refuses both. His discriminating application to every kind of hearer, from the unteachable to the fallen believer, recovers preaching as a pastoral and converting ordinance, not a weekly speech. The power lies not in the man but in the Word he opens and the Spirit who carries it home.
roots_summary: The title uses “prophesying” in its biblical sense of preaching the Word, and “art” as a teachable, ordered method.
roots_lines: Greek prophēteuō — to prophesy, here to speak forth God’s Word in edification, as in 1 Corinthians 14.
The older English prophesying — the public exposition and application of Scripture in preaching.
English art — a skilled and teachable method, a discipline that can be learned.
Perkins’s Latin original bore the title Prophetica.
The method moves from text, to sense, to doctrine, to use or application.
usage: Perkins’s manual is cited as the fountainhead of the Puritan plain style of preaching.
His taxonomy of hearers is taught to train ministers in discriminating application.
The work is recommended to preachers recovering expository, text-driven preaching.

etymology: From Latin De Consolatione Philosophiae; consolation (comfort in distress) and philosophy (the love of wisdom); the work of Boethius.
biblical_def: The Consolation of Philosophy is the famous work written by the Roman senator and Christian Boethius while imprisoned and awaiting execution in the early sixth century. In it the figure of Lady Philosophy visits the condemned man in his cell and reasons with him concerning the fickleness of Fortune, the emptiness of earthly goods, the nature of true happiness, the providence of God, the problem of evil, and the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human freedom. The book became one of the most influential and widely read works of the Middle Ages, treasured for its serene wisdom in the face of death and its meditation on the unchanging good above the turning wheel of Fortune. The dictionary honors Boethius as a confessing Christian who suffered unjustly and met death with composure, and as a thinker who handed down much that the church found useful. Yet it marks plainly that the Consolation is a work of philosophy, not of the gospel: Christ is not named, the cross is absent, and the comfort offered rises no higher than reason can climb. The Christian’s true consolation in prison and at the scaffold is not the cold serenity of philosophy but the living hope of the gospel—not the wheel of Fortune abandoned for an abstract Good, but the providence of a Father who works all things together for good to them that love God.
webster_summary: Boethius’s celebrated sixth-century work, written in prison, on Fortune, providence, and true happiness; honored for its serene wisdom, but rising only as high as reason, not the gospel.
webster_full: THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY, the work of Boethius, written in prison awaiting execution.
Lady Philosophy reasons with the condemned man on Fortune, happiness, providence, and evil.
One of the most read and influential books of the Middle Ages.
Treasured for its composure in the face of unjust death and its meditation on the unchanging good.
A work of philosophy, not the gospel—Christ unnamed, the cross absent, the comfort that of reason.

Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Philosophy is mistaken for the gospel—a natural wisdom and serenity offered as if it could console the soul as Christ alone can.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the elevation of philosophy into a rival or a substitute for the gospel—the ancient and ever-renewed confidence that human reason, unaided, can find the highest good, master the fear of death, and console the dying soul. Boethius’s book, for all its beauty, illustrates the limit: it climbs as high as the natural light can reach, to an unchanging Good and an ordering Providence, but it does not reach Calvary. The world by wisdom knew not God; it pleased God to save by the preaching of the cross, which the Greeks counted foolishness.

The dictionary honors Boethius the man—a Christian who suffered injustice and died with dignity—while refusing to let his most famous work stand in for the consolation it never names. Paul warns the Colossians to beware lest any spoil them through philosophy and vain deceit, not after Christ. The believer facing death has a better comfort than Lady Philosophy can give: not the abandonment of Fortune for an abstract Good, but a crucified and risen Saviour, and a Father whose providence is not a turning wheel but a fixed and fatherly purpose working all things for the good of His own.
roots_summary: The title joins comfort in distress with the love of wisdom, naming a consolation that reason can reach but the gospel surpasses.
roots_lines: Latin consolatio — comfort, solace in grief or distress.
Greek philosophia — the love of wisdom, the disciplined pursuit of truth by reason.
The original title, De Consolatione Philosophiae, “on the consolation of philosophy.”
Boethius personifies Philosophy as a noble lady who instructs the prisoner.
The work stands at the boundary of classical philosophy and the Christian Middle Ages.
usage: Boethius’s Consolation is studied as a bridge between classical and medieval thought.
It is cited to mark the difference between natural wisdom and the gospel’s comfort.
Its meditation on providence and foreknowledge is discussed in the history of that doctrine.

etymology: From Latin De Civitate Dei; city (a commonwealth, a body of citizens) and God; Augustine’s great treatise contrasting the two cities.
biblical_def: The City of God is the great work of Augustine of Hippo, begun after the sack of Rome in the early fifth century, when pagans charged that the abandonment of the old gods for Christ had brought the empire low. Augustine answered with a vast meditation on history, dividing all mankind into two cities distinguished by two loves: the earthly city, built by the love of self even to the contempt of God, and the heavenly city, built by the love of God even to the contempt of self. These two cities, intermingled in this present age, run through all history from the fall to the last judgment, when they shall be finally separated—the one to everlasting punishment, the other to eternal life. Augustine demolished the pretensions of pagan religion and philosophy, expounded the providence of God over the rise and fall of empires, and set the believer’s true citizenship in heaven, a pilgrim in the earthly city but a member of the city that has foundations. The dictionary honors Augustine as the greatest of the Latin fathers, whose doctrine of grace the Reformers gladly claimed, and whose two-cities framework remains a profound guide to the Christian’s posture in the world. Some elements of his ecclesiology were later pressed in directions the Reformation rejected, but the central vision—two cities, two loves, one final judgment—is biblical and enduring.
webster_summary: Augustine’s monumental treatise contrasting the earthly city, built on love of self, with the heavenly city, built on love of God—two cities running through all history to the last judgment.
webster_full: THE CITY OF GOD, the great treatise of Augustine of Hippo.
Written after the sack of Rome to answer the charge that Christianity had ruined the empire.
Divides mankind into two cities marked by two loves—love of self and love of God.
Traces the two cities, intermingled now, through history to their final separation.
Sets the believer’s true citizenship in heaven, a pilgrim in the earthly city.
scriptures: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
corruption_summary: Augustine’s two-cities vision is flattened into mere politics, or its doctrine of grace is severed from the medieval church that misapplied his ecclesiology.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the antithesis of the two cities: all history is the contest of two loves, the love of self that builds Babylon and the love of God that builds Jerusalem, intermingled until the judgment divides them forever. Against the modern reduction of Augustine to a political theorist or a culture-warrior on either side, the dictionary keeps his vision eschatological—the believer is a pilgrim whose citizenship is in heaven and who here has no continuing city.

A discerning reader honors Augustine’s doctrine of grace, which the Reformers claimed as their own against the Pelagians, while marking that his identification of the city of God with the visible church was later pressed by Rome into a defense of papal and ecclesiastical power the Reformation rightly rejected. The corruption is not in Augustine’s central vision but in its later misuse to exalt the institutional church. The two cities are not Rome and the barbarians, nor church and state simply, but the company of the redeemed and the company of the lost, known finally to God alone.
roots_summary: The title sets the city of God against the earthly city, naming two commonwealths divided by their loves and destined for opposite ends.
roots_lines: Latin civitas — a city, a commonwealth, a body of citizens; the title word.
The original, De Civitate Dei contra Paganos, “on the city of God against the pagans.”
The biblical “city of God” — Zion, Jerusalem, and the heavenly city of Hebrews 11 and 12.
Augustine’s two cities are marked by amor sui, love of self, and amor Dei, love of God.
The framework draws on Babylon and Jerusalem as the two cities of Scripture.
usage: Augustine’s two-cities framework is foundational for Christian reflection on history and politics.
The City of God is cited for the believer’s heavenly citizenship and pilgrim posture.
Reformed writers claim Augustine’s doctrine of grace while critiquing his later ecclesial misuse.

etymology: From thesis (Greek, a proposition set down for disputation); the ninety-five propositions Luther offered for academic debate.
biblical_def: The Ninety-Five Theses, properly the Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences, were the ninety-five propositions Martin Luther posted at Wittenberg on the eve of All Saints in the autumn of 1517, an event widely reckoned the spark of the Protestant Reformation. Written in Latin for academic disputation, they protested the sale of indulgences—papal pardons hawked by Tetzel with the jingle that as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs. Luther argued that the pope had no power to remit guilt, that true repentance is the whole life of the believer, that the treasury of the church is the gospel of the grace of God, and that the Christian who truly repents has full remission of penalty and guilt without indulgence letters. The Theses spread across Germany within weeks by the new printing press, igniting a controversy that Luther himself had not foreseen and that soon grew from a protest against an abuse into a recovery of the gospel of justification by faith alone. The dictionary marks the Ninety-Five Theses as the providential beginning of the Reformation, though Luther’s own theology was still maturing when he wrote them—they protest an abuse more than they yet proclaim the full doctrine of grace. Their abiding worth is the principle they assert: that pardon is God’s free gift in Christ, not the church’s merchandise.
webster_summary: The ninety-five propositions Martin Luther posted at Wittenberg in 1517 against the sale of indulgences, widely reckoned the spark of the Protestant Reformation.
webster_full: NINETY-FIVE THESES, Luther’s disputation on the power and efficacy of indulgences, 1517.
Posted at Wittenberg for academic debate, written in Latin, against the sale of pardons.
Protested Tetzel’s indulgence traffic and the claim that money could release souls from purgatory.
Asserted that true repentance is lifelong and that pardon is God’s free gift, not the church’s merchandise.
Spread by the printing press across Germany, igniting the Reformation.
scriptures: Rom 1:17
For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Act 8:20
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
corruption_summary: The indulgence traffic that Luther opposed was itself the corruption—the selling of God’s free pardon as the church’s merchandise.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the historic one the Theses oppose: the Roman traffic in indulgences, by which the free forgiveness of God in Christ was turned into a commodity to be purchased, the fear of purgatory exploited for the building of basilicas, and the treasury of merit substituted for the finished work of the cross. Luther’s protest recovered the principle that pardon is God’s gift, bought by Christ’s blood and received by faith, never by the coin in the coffer.

A modern corruption sentimentalizes the event into a tale of one brave man against the system, while emptying it of doctrine—as if Luther stood merely for individual conscience or institutional reform rather than for the gospel. The dictionary keeps the substance: the Reformation was not first a revolt but a recovery, the rediscovery that the just shall live by faith and that the gift of God cannot be purchased with money. Luther’s theology was still ripening in 1517; the Theses protest an abuse more than they yet proclaim the full doctrine of justification, but the seed of the whole Reformation is in them.
roots_summary: The title names the ninety-five propositions set down for disputation, the academic spark of a gospel recovery.
roots_lines: Greek thesis — a proposition or position set down, especially one offered for debate.
The Latin title: Disputatio pro declaratione virtutis indulgentiarum.
Indulgence — in Roman teaching, a remission of temporal penalty for sin, here sold for money.
Posted on the eve of All Saints, 31 October 1517, at the Castle Church door in Wittenberg.
The printing press carried them across Germany within weeks, beyond Luther’s intent.
usage: The posting of the Ninety-Five Theses is commemorated annually on Reformation Day.
They are cited as the spark, though not the full doctrine, of the Protestant Reformation.
Their protest against indulgences is contrasted with the gospel of free justification.
